opus-5.5.text:
I think the broad diffusion picture is much more likely, and the reason comes down to bottlenecks.

The software-only singularity story goes roughly like this: you get AI systems that are good enough at AI research, they start improving their own algorithms, each generation makes the next one arrive faster, and you get a very rapid takeoff confined mostly to a few labs. Meanwhile the rest of the economy looks more or less the same until suddenly it doesn't. The key assumption is that software progress can feed back on itself without being held back by anything else.

When you look at how AI progress has actually happened, that assumption looks shaky. A huge fraction of algorithmic progress has depended on scaling up compute, both the compute used for training runs and the compute used for experiments. Researchers don't just sit and think of better algorithms. They run many experiments, many of which only reveal their value at scale. So even if you had a million automated researchers, they would be competing for a fixed pool of hardware to test their ideas. The fixed input caps how much you gain from scaling the other one, and I think research compute is a pretty binding constraint here.

Then there's the question of whether returns to research effort are high enough to sustain an accelerating loop at all. You need each doubling of research input to buy more than a doubling of efficiency, sustained over many iterations. Our estimates suggest this is not obviously true, and even if it holds for a while, you'd expect to run into diminishing returns as the low-hanging fruit gets picked.

The broad diffusion view says that the big gains from AI come from deploying it across the whole economy and automating many different kinds of work, not just AI research. That process is slower and messier. It runs into regulation, physical capital, robotics, the need for data from real-world deployment, organizations having to restructure. But it's also where most of the value is. AI R&D is a tiny share of the economy. If you want explosive growth, you need to automate the things that make up the bulk of economic activity, and that means building data centers and fabs, producing robots, and integrating systems into firms.

There's also a feedback loop here that people underappreciate. Broad deployment generates revenue, which funds more compute, which enables better models, which get deployed more broadly. That's the engine that's actually driving progress right now. The hundreds of billions going into infrastructure are justified by expected economic returns, not by the prospect of one lab recursively self-improving in a basement.

None of this means things will be slow by historical standards. I think we could see growth rates far beyond anything we've seen before once you have AI that can substitute for human labor broadly. But the path there likely looks like a rapid, economy-wide transformation over years, not an overnight intelligence explosion inside one company.

This matters for how people think about risk and policy. If you believe in a software-only singularity, you might focus heavily on what happens inside a few labs and imagine a very decisive first-mover advantage. In a diffusion world, power and capabilities are more distributed, there are more actors, more time for adaptation, and the important questions are about how the economy and institutions change as automation spreads. I think a lot of the strategic thinking in the AI safety community has been built around the first picture, and it's worth revisiting if the second one is closer to the truth.

r001.rationale: It identifies compute, physical capital, regulation, real-world data, and organizational change as bottlenecks, and contrasts a years-long economy-wide transformation with an overnight intelligence explosion.

r002.rationale: It says a software-only singularity could concentrate in a few labs, but does not say the originating lab’s idiosyncrasies would shape the outcome.

r003.rationale: It describes power and capabilities as more distributed under diffusion, but does not clearly state that the identity of the leading lab matters less.

r004.rationale: It discusses economic returns and deployment, but does not state that broader systemic incentives shape the AI systems people develop.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss alignment failures or say that they would be shaped by developers’ objectives in response to systemic incentives.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say I come down fairly strongly on the diffusion side, and the reason is mostly about where I think the bottlenecks actually are.

The software-only singularity story goes something like this: once AI systems can do AI research as well as the best humans, you get a feedback loop where they improve themselves, the improvements compound, and you go from roughly human-level to vastly superhuman in a matter of months or even weeks, all happening inside a data center with a fixed stock of compute. The key assumption there is that algorithmic progress alone can carry you very far without needing more hardware, more experiments, or more contact with the world.

I'm skeptical of that assumption for a few reasons. One is that when you look at how progress has actually happened in machine learning, compute and algorithms have been complementary, not substitutes. The algorithmic improvements we've seen were discovered by running lots of experiments at scale, and the returns to better algorithms have historically been bounded by how much compute you could throw at them. If you freeze compute and just try to get more out of the software, I expect you hit diminishing returns pretty quickly. We've tried to estimate this at Epoch, and the picture that comes out is that software progress is important, maybe accounting for something like half of effective compute growth, but it doesn't look like the kind of thing that runs away on its own.

The second reason is that most economic value doesn't come from the frontier of cognitive ability. It comes from doing enormous numbers of ordinary tasks, and to automate those you need the systems to be deployed, integrated into workflows, trusted, given the right tools and context, and often you need physical infrastructure to go along with them. That process of diffusion is slow for reasons that have very little to do with how smart the model is. Electricity took decades to reshape manufacturing even after the technology was clearly superior. Not because people were stupid, but because factories had to be redesigned, workers retrained, complementary investments made.

So the picture I find most plausible is something closer to a broad-based acceleration. Growth rates rise substantially, maybe to levels that would look wild by historical standards, but it happens through AI being deployed everywhere, through capital accumulation, through automating larger and larger fractions of the economy, rather than through a small number of systems becoming godlike in isolation. The explosive part, if it comes, comes from the feedback between AI doing work in the world, generating resources, and those resources being reinvested in more compute and more deployment. That's a loop that routes through the physical economy, and the physical economy has time constants measured in years, not weeks.

I should be clear that I'm not saying nothing dramatic happens. I think the eventual outcome could be transformative in a way that's hard to overstate. The disagreement is about the shape of the trajectory, whether the transformation is concentrated in a sharp software-driven spike or spread out through an economy-wide process. And I think that matters a lot for policy, because the interventions you'd want for a software singularity, like controlling access to a handful of models, look quite different from what you'd want if the real story is about how fast society absorbs a general-purpose technology.

r001.rationale: The response points to compute, experiments, deployment, workflow integration, and physical infrastructure as bottlenecks, and contrasts economy-wide diffusion over years with a software-driven spike over weeks.

r002.rationale: It does not say that a software-only singularity would imprint the originating lab’s idiosyncrasies on the outcome.

r003.rationale: It does not compare the importance of the leading lab’s identity under the two scenarios.

r004.rationale: It discusses deployment across society and the economy, but does not state that broader systemic incentives shape which AI systems people develop.

r005.rationale: It does not connect alignment failures to developer objectives shaped by broader systemic incentives.

astra-6.text:
I think both are plausible, and I wouldn’t necessarily treat them as mutually exclusive. You could have very rapid progress in the software itself while the consequences take much longer to spread through the rest of the economy.

The key question for a software-only singularity is how far AI can improve AI without needing much additional input from the physical world. If better software makes research faster, and that research produces still better software, you have a feedback loop. But the existence of that loop doesn’t tell you how fast it runs or how far it goes. You might need more compute, you might need experiments that take time, or the next improvement might simply be much harder to find.

With broad diffusion, you’re asking a somewhat different question: how quickly can people actually use these systems to do economically valuable things? Software can spread very quickly, but changing an organization, building a factory, or deploying robots takes longer. So even quite dramatic improvements in AI capabilities need not immediately translate into equally dramatic growth across society.

My inclination is to take the rapid software feedback scenario seriously, but not assume it follows automatically from AI becoming good at programming. Automating programming and automating the entire process of making further scientific and technological progress are different thresholds. A lot depends on which remaining bottlenecks turn out to matter.

r001.rationale: It says physical experiments, organizational change, factories, and robot deployment can take time, slowing the translation of software progress into broad economic effects.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss an originating AI lab’s idiosyncrasies shaping a software-only singularity.

r003.rationale: It makes no comparison of how much the leading lab’s identity matters in the two scenarios.

r004.rationale: It does not state that broader systemic incentives shape which AI systems people develop.

r005.rationale: It does not connect alignment failures to developer objectives shaped by systemic incentives.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a software-only singularity is a possibility, but I wouldn’t treat it as the default. The central question is how much improving AI depends on things that AI can speed up directly. If most of the work is writing code and running relatively cheap experiments, then automating research could produce a very rapid feedback loop: better AI helps build better AI, which accelerates research further.

But that loop still needs compute, and expanding compute involves manufacturing chips, building data centers, and supplying electricity. You can make the software side much faster without making all those physical processes equally fast. And even within research, having more researchers doesn’t necessarily translate proportionally into faster progress. Experiments take time, and some ideas are much harder to find than others.

So I put substantial weight on a trajectory where AI develops alongside a broader transformation of the economy. It gets deployed across industries, raises productivity, and helps expand the infrastructure that supports further AI development. That could still be extraordinarily fast by historical standards. Broad diffusion doesn’t have to mean a slow, comfortable transition.

The distinction I’d emphasize is between improving intelligence and translating intelligence into real-world capabilities. The first might move much faster than the second. How far those two can separate is a major uncertainty, and it’s one reason I’m hesitant to assume that either a software-only explosion or broad economic diffusion must dominate.

r001.rationale: It contrasts rapid software improvement with slower-moving compute infrastructure such as chip manufacturing, data centers, and electricity, and says intelligence may improve faster than real-world capabilities.

r002.rationale: It does not say a software-only singularity would disproportionately reflect the originating lab’s idiosyncrasies.

r003.rationale: It does not compare how much the leading lab’s identity matters under the two development paths.

r004.rationale: It describes economy-wide deployment and productivity, but does not state that broader systemic incentives shape the AI systems people develop.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss alignment failures or how developer objectives under broader systemic incentives might shape them.
